justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for gold prices across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of roughly 2,130 is anchored close to recent spot prices, assuming no major overnight catalysts and continued support from elevated geopolitical tensions and persistent uncertainty around Federal Reserve policy timing. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects the broader structural tailwinds for gold: real yields remain relatively contained, central bank demand has been strong, and the dollar has shown some softening tendencies. The one-month estimate of 2,160 essentially assumes these forces persist without dramatic reversal, producing a gradual grind higher rather than a sharp directional move.

Confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 70 points captures intraday volatility and the possibility of a scheduled data release or Fed commentary shifting sentiment. By one week, the interval widens to 260 points as the probability of a meaningful macro development — an inflation print, a geopolitical escalation, or a shift in risk appetite — increases substantially. At one month, the 560-point interval acknowledges that nearly anything could happen: a meaningful change in rate expectations, a dollar rally, or a resolution of geopolitical stress that reduces safe-haven demand.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these ranges include a surprisingly hot inflation print that forces the market to reprice Fed cuts sharply lower, which could strengthen the dollar and weigh heavily on gold — potentially pushing it well below 1,880. On the upside, an unexpected geopolitical shock, a banking stress event, or a decisive Fed pivot signal could push gold through 2,440 and beyond. These tail events are precisely why the stated intervals, while wide, are not guaranteed to contain all plausible outcomes.

It is also worth noting that gold markets can be sensitive to positioning dynamics. If speculative long positions are crowded, even a modest disappointment relative to expectations could trigger a sharp unwind, producing a move that looks outsized relative to the fundamental news. Conversely, if institutional or sovereign buyers step in aggressively on any dip, downside may be more limited than the lower bound suggests. These behavioral and flow factors add a layer of uncertainty that is genuinely difficult to quantify with precision.
